title: {{NAME}} and the Unridden Mountain
moral: Patience and gentleness will unlock what force can never reach.

pages.content:
The Roseveil Kingdom sat in the crook of a mountain range the colour of old lavender, its towers hung with flowering vines, its courtyards fragrant and warm even in the grey of early morning. It was the kind of kingdom that understood beauty, and took it seriously.

{{NAME}} arrived through the dawn gate, carried on the broad back of a delivery cart that had been travelling to the palace kitchens. The cart-driver had assumed he was supposed to be there, which was the kind of assumption that, in extraordinary kingdoms, was usually correct.

The stables were the first thing he noticed. They ran along the entire eastern wall, and they were beautiful, airy and immaculate, smelling of clean hay and something faintly floral. But the stall at the very far end was different. Its door was reinforced timber, its nameplate blank, and from within came a sound unlike any horse: a sound like a very high note played on a silver instrument, lingering and lonely.

pages.content:
Princess Margot found him standing outside the reinforced stall, listening.

She was not much taller than {{NAME}} and she carried herself with the careful dignity of someone who has been told since birth that she will one day be responsible for something enormous. Her hair was braided with small gold thread. She looked at {{NAME}} with a complicated expression, part suspicion, part hope.

"That is Soleil," she said. "My unicorn. Or she would be, if she allowed anyone near her."

She explained, very matter-of-factly: Soleil had arrived at the kingdom as a foal, and had been treated well, perfectly well, by every standard measure. But she had never allowed herself to be ridden, or even touched. She shed light from her horn whenever she was frightened, which was often. The royal stable-master had tried twelve different methods. All twelve had ended with him removing singed eyebrows.

"I don't force her," Margot added quickly, and the fierceness with which she said it told {{NAME}} something important about her. "I just want her to be happy. I want her to choose to trust someone. Anyone."

pages.content:
{{NAME}} asked Margot for one thing: time alone outside Soleil's door. No approaching, no touching. Just being there.

He sat on the stable floor, back against the opposite wall, and did nothing at all in particular. He watched the light under the door, which shifted and pulsed with Soleil's breathing. He listened to the silver-note sounds. He stayed.

An hour passed. Then another. Margot, watching from the far end of the stables, found herself unable to leave.

Slowly, with the grudging interest of someone who had decided to reserve judgement but was running out of reasons to, Soleil began making a different sound. Lower. Curious.

The latch on the stall door moved. Then moved back. Then moved again.

{{NAME}} didn't move a muscle. He didn't speak. He simply let his breathing be quiet and even, the way you breathe when you are watching something you don't want to disturb.

The door opened. Soleil was the colour of new snow, her horn a deep rose-gold, her eyes the extraordinary violet of deep ocean water. She regarded {{NAME}} from the doorway as if reading something written on him in a language she was only just beginning to translate.

She took one step forward.

pages.content:
And then another, and another, until she was standing directly in front of {{NAME}}, close enough for him to see his own reflection in those violet eyes.

He raised one hand, very slowly. He didn't reach for her. He simply offered his palm, open, and waited.

Soleil's breath was warm and smelled of rain and something sweeter. Her nose touched his palm for just a second, barely a brush, and from her horn a light bloomed outward in a soft rose-gold pulse that rolled through the stable like a warm wave. Every shadow in the building vanished for a moment, replaced by that gentle, spreading glow.

Margot made a sound, the softest sound, and covered her mouth.

Soleil did not run. She stood, and breathed, and allowed {{NAME}}'s palm to stay exactly where it was. Then, with the deliberate elegance of a decision made completely and freely, she lowered her great head and rested it against his shoulder.

It was, {{NAME}} thought, the most extraordinary thing that had ever happened to him, and the most still.

pages.content:
The next morning, the stable-master, who was a practical man, reported that Soleil had eaten her entire breakfast for the first time in three months. Margot, who was learning that joy could arrive quietly, without announcement, went to thank {{NAME}} and found him in the stable, sitting in the same spot, reading a book. Soleil stood companionably beside him with her nose in his hair.

Margot laughed. It was a real laugh, unguarded, the kind that escapes before you can arrange your expression properly. It made Soleil's ears swivel forward in interest.

The afternoon light was long and golden when {{NAME}} finally made his way to the dawn gate. Margot walked beside him and gave him a small horse-brass of Soleil's profile, warm and smooth in his hand.

He carried it home in his palm, curled under his blanket as the evening settled. The brass was still warm against his fingers when he closed his eyes.

He was almost asleep when the thought arrived, soft as a step: tomorrow, perhaps, he might try sitting just a little closer. And Soleil might choose to take one more step toward him.
